lead: Today's readings ask who sets us at liberty. Paul says every person serves some master, and that the service of sin pays its wages in death, while God gives eternal life as a gift. In Matthew, a paralysed man is carried to Jesus, and before his legs are healed his sins are forgiven. The key words are slave, gift and authority.

set: Paul has been saying that where sin increased, grace abounded even more (5:20). Someone may then ask whether it matters how we behave. Romans 6 answers: in Baptism we died with Christ to sin (6:3–4). In this section Paul uses the picture of slavery, which every reader in a Roman city would know at first hand. He apologises for the comparison in v. 19. He is using a social fact to make a point, and is not approving of slavery.
str: vv. 16–19: two masters; once slaves of sin, now of righteousness.
vv. 20–22: what each service produced: shame and death, or holiness and life.
v. 23: the summary: wages and gift.
kw: The word means one who belongs wholly to another. In Paul it can be a title of honour; he calls himself “a servant” of Jesus Christ in this very letter (Romans 1:1, where the Greek word is the same).
This was a word for a soldier's pay. Sin keeps its promises in the worst way: it pays exactly what it owes.
This is the opposite of wages. Nobody earns it. Paul sets the two words side by side on purpose.
vv: But thanks be to God that you, having once been slaves of sin, have become obedient from the heart to the form of teaching to which you were entrusted,

Notice the unusual turn of phrase. Paul does not say the teaching was entrusted to them but that they were entrusted to the teaching. Many scholars think he has in mind the instruction given before Baptism.
So what advantage did you then get from the things of which you now are ashamed?
This is a question for a good examination of conscience. Paul does not argue from fear here. He asks what sin ever really gave us.
For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
The Malayalam POC divides the verses a little differently and puts the first half of this sentence at the end of v. 22.
ch: The Catechism says that the more we do what is good the freer we become, and that the choice of evil is an abuse of freedom that leads to “the slavery of sin” (CCC 1733). Death is a consequence of sin (CCC 1008). St Augustine often repeats that when God crowns our merits he is crowning his own gifts (in substance), and this is the sense of Paul's last verse (compare CCC 2006–2009).

r.h: Authority on earth to forgive sins
set: “His own town” is Capernaum, where Jesus has settled (4:13). Mark and Luke tell this story too, with the crowd and the opening of the roof (Mark 2:1–12; Luke 5:17–26). Matthew tells it briefly and keeps only what matters most: the faith of those who bring him, the word of forgiveness, the objection, and the sign.
str: vv. 1–2: the man is brought, and Jesus forgives him.
vv. 3–4: the scribes' thought and Jesus' question.
kw: The same word that Jesus speaks to the disciples on the sea (14:27). He speaks courage first, before the cure.
The crowds have already noticed this in his teaching (7:29). Now it reaches to sin itself.
Jesus' own title for himself. It recalls the figure in Daniel 7:13–14, to whom authority is given.
vv: When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven.”
“Their faith” means the faith of those who carried him. Others can bring someone to Christ when that person cannot go alone, and this is what intercession does.
Then some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming.”
They are thinking seriously, for only God forgives sins. Their objection states the very truth that the story reveals about Jesus (CCC 589).
When the crowds saw it, they were filled with awe, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings.
Only Matthew ends this way, and the plural is striking. Many commentators hear in it the Church of Matthew's own day, in which this authority continues (compare 16:19; 18:18).
ch: The Catechism teaches that only God forgives sins, that Jesus exercises this divine power as Son of God, and that he gives it to men to exercise in his name (CCC 1441). It names Christ the physician of souls and bodies who forgave and healed this man, and it says that he wills his Church to continue this healing in the sacraments (CCC 1421). St Ambrose marvels at a Lord who pardons one person for the sake of others' merit (in substance; On Luke 5).

qa: Does Jesus mean that the man's illness was caused by his sins?
Not in this passage. Elsewhere Jesus rejects that simple link (John 9:2–3; Luke 13:1–5). Here he addresses the deepest need first, and then shows his authority by the healing that can be seen.
study: Who has carried me to Christ, and whom am I carrying now in my prayer?
Romans 6:21 asks what advantage sin ever gave me. How would I honestly answer before my next confession?
